newsitem.title: BELARUS: Standoff goes on in Belarus despite Russia talks.
newsitem.headline: Standoff goes on in Belarus despite Russia talks.

text.p: Prospects for a compromise between President Alexander Lukashenko and his parliamentary opponents dimmed on Thursday after the Belarussian leader snubbed a Russian peace initiative.

Lukashenko, who stayed away from talks with Russian parliamentary leaders in Smolensk late on Wednesday, pressed ahead with plans to visit the western city of Brest in his campaign for a referendum on Sunday to widen his powers.
Parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky, spokesman for the president's critics, agreed with Lukashenko early on Thursday to meet later in the day.
"Sharetsky and Lukashenko talked by telephone and Lukashenko said he would call him as soon as he flew into Minsk and they would meet," Sharetsky aide Vladikmir Ulakhovich said.
But chances of a compromise being found seemed slim as there was no sign of either side backing down on its demands.
Aides said Lukashenko was too busy to attend the Smolensk talks with Sharetsky and the two Russian speakers, who appealed for a compromise deal on reforming the Belarussian constitution.

Lukashenko, in a late-night interview on state television, said Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin might fly straight to Minsk from an official visit to Murmansk on Friday, though there was no confirmation from the Russian side.

Sharetsky told deputies that the Smolensk talks had decided a solution should be found respecting the constitution and laws of the former Soviet republic of 10 million which borders Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine.

Meanwhile the 42-year-old president remained defiant, making clear he was not interested in the Smolensk peace formula, which would have required him to call off the referendum, for which early voting began on November 9.
A crowd of protesters -- mostly nationalists opposed to the president's pro-Russian stance and his derisive comments on the Belarussian language -- kept up a vigil outside parliament.
Hundreds of people have stood on Independence Square each day since Thursday last week, when Lukashenko sacked the electoral commission head appointed by parliament.
Organisers said 20 people were hurt when demonstrators clashed with police on Sunday.

Yuri Zakharenko, a former interior minister -- one of several senior officials who have been sacked or resigned in recent months -- told reporters the police and crack interior ministry forces were in a state of combat readiness in case of trouble.
Lukashenko, who usually appears in public in a severe dark grey suit, seemed more relaxed in his Thursday night interview in an open-necked shirt and sweater.
But he made clear that even after pressure from the Kremlin, including a long conversation on Wednesday with President Boris Yeltsin, he would not soften his position.
His main demand is that parliament should abandon plans to impeach him.
The Belarus constitutional court, whose rulings the president has repeatedly ignored, is to meet on Friday to discuss the impeachment bid, launched by 70 deputies.

Lukashenko has the support of enough deputies to be able to stop the impeachment bid succeeding at the final stage. His opponents cannot muster the two-thirds majority of the 199 deputies required to remove him from office.
Lukashenko is seeking popular backing for major changes to the constitution which would extend his term by more than two years and tighten his grip on rival institutions.
An aide hinted that Lukashenko would dissolve parliament and the court if they tried to unseat the president, though according to the present constitution he has no right to do so.
"I will not give up this power...There must be order in the country...Power must be in strong hands to be strong, not in shaky, drunken hands," Lukashenko said on Wednesday.

"Almost four million people voted for the president, and 70 deputies and a few constitutional court judges...will vote to remove the president from power. Surely, that's absurd? Of course it's absurd," he told the interviewer.
"Yes indeed, the people did not give me power so I could give it up to some political pirates," he said.
